To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Mn2+ is taken up into the brain from the circulation by a mechanism that is critically affected by Mn2+ binding to plasma proteins.
manganese is rapidly taken up into brain and choroidal plexus from blood and that this uptake is facilitated by a mechanism that is critically affected by the free fraction of manganese in blood.

manganese(II) is readily taken up across the blood‐blood barrier, that uptake from the blood is limited by the plasma proteins that bind manganese(II) and that transport is facilitated, either by an active or passive mechanism.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the mechanisms by which the central nervous system regulates its own blood flow.
the development of new methods for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases, such as Parkinson’s disease.
the development of a new class of compounds, called “metallosurfactants,” which are composed of a metal complex and an amphiphilic ligand.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of the study are consistent with the hypothesis that Mn transport across the blood brain barrier is facilitated by an active or a facilitated process.
Mn2+ is readily transported across the blood–brain barrier, and the transport mechanism is critically affected by the binding of the metal to plasma proteins.
the blood‐brain transfer of Mn2+ is rapid and that the mechanism of this transfer is not passive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

Mn(II) transport across the BBB occurs by facilitated diffusion, which is critically affected by Mn(II) binding to plasma proteins, and that the facilitated diffusion is not due to the presence of a Mn(II) carrier.
Mn(II) transport across the BBB is facilitated by a carrier-mediated mechanism that is sensitive to the presence of plasma proteins, particularly transferrin.

the Mn2+ transport is facilitated by either a carrier mediated or an active transport mechanism, and the transport is critically affected not only by plasma protein binding, but also by other factors such as the presence of competing metal ions, pH, and ionic strength of the medium.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the blood‐brain-barrier can allow for rapid Mn2+ uptake into the brain, which may have implications for the use of Mn2+‐based contrast agents in MRI.
Mn2+ is readily transported across the blood‐ brain barrier and that the rate of uptake is dependent upon the free Mn2+ in the blood, which is determined by plasma protein binding.
Mn2+ is readily transported into the brain and that its transport can be significantly restricted by plasma protein binding.
